design_detail: Practice Pointer in the BMJ (published online 19 February 2014; four pages, 20 references) by three consultant toxicologists in Sydney and Newcastle, Australia; commissioned and externally peer reviewed. There is no methods section: no search or selection is described. Question-and-answer format (What is serotonin syndrome? How does it present? How do we diagnose it? How can we treat it? How can we prevent it?), with a box of drugs, summary points, a figure of the spectrum of effects and a flowchart of the Hunter criteria. The treatment section gives doses, which this card does not record.
can_establish: How three toxicologists described in 2014 what serotonin toxicity is, how it presents and is recognised, which drug classes have been linked to it, and what they take the case literature to show about which combinations produce severe toxicity; it points to primary sources.
cannot_establish: How often any combination causes serotonin toxicity or death (no rate is given for any pair); whether the Hunter criteria have been independently validated in the sense the word implies (only the paper that derived them is cited); whether nearly all severe cases involving a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is a feature of the disorder or of what has been published; or anything about pairs the chosen literature does not cover.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review; no search described). The figures it gives come from the authors’ own group: a large case series of SSRI overdoses (moderate toxicity in 15%, no severe cases; reference 5) and a series of moclobemide overdoses (reference 15, not read for this library). The statement that nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI rests on six cited reviews of case reports, four of them by one author (references 3, 4, 9 and 10, Gillman).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated: no criteria for choosing the 20 references.
sample.selection_effects: The review’s central generalisation rests on published case reports and reviews of them, which record what was noticed and published, and on one toxicology group’s overdose series; people with mild toxicity and people who took mixes that were never written up would not appear.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Drug exposure is described as listed in Box 1 and in the cited literature.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the causes. The treatment section gives doses, which are not recorded in this library.
exposure.polysubstance: The review says severe toxicity usually occurs only with a combination of two or more serotonergic drugs (even when each is at a therapeutic dose), one of which is generally an MAOI; that interactions of an SSRI with any MAOI might be lethal; that interactions with other serotonin reuptake inhibitors are likely to be minor and interactions with serotonin-releasing agents such as amphetamines might even attenuate toxicity (one cited volunteer study of citalopram with MDMA, reference 18, not read); and that moclobemide overdose alone did not produce toxicity, while with a second serotonergic drug toxicity was nearly always present and severe in about half (reference 15, not read).

outcomes.instruments: Clinical diagnosis by the triad of neuromuscular, autonomic and mental-status features, and the Hunter criteria (Figure 2) to confirm moderate or severe toxicity.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review says the Hunter criteria have been validated and cites one source for this, the paper that derived them (reference 13, Dunkley and colleagues, two of whose authors are authors of this review).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed. Moderate toxicity is described as occurring in 15% of SSRI overdoses; severe toxicity as a rapidly rising temperature with rigidity.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new analysis. Figures quoted, mostly from the authors’ own group: moderate serotonin toxicity in 15% of SSRI poisonings, with no severe cases (reference 5); no toxicity in overdoses of moclobemide alone, but with a second serotonergic drug toxicity nearly always present and severe in about half (reference 15); mortality below 1% when the supportive approaches described had been applied (references 5 and 15); in the spectrum figure, multiples of 3 to 5, 5 to 10 and 10 to 100 for the rise in serotonin efflux seen in animal models, set against mild, moderate and severe toxicity.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged. The review says spurious associations and cautions have proliferated elsewhere and that product information impedes sensible decision support, and names a few interactions it regards as unsupported (carbamazepine, most tricyclic and atypical antidepressants, triptans), without listing the evidence for each.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A practice-oriented synthesis, by authors whose own units produced much of the data, of what serotonin toxicity is, how it is recognised and which drugs are implicated, concluding that severe toxicity usually needs a combination of serotonergic drugs, generally including an MAOI; no rate is given for any pair.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review says the Hunter criteria have been validated (p. 2), that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (p. 3), that an SSRI with any MAOI might be lethal (p. 3), and that interactions of an SSRI with serotonin-releasing agents such as amphetamines might even attenuate toxicity (p. 3). Gaps: (1) validated rests on the derivation paper alone, by two of this review’s three authors’ group, with no independent test cited; (2) the MAOI statement rests on reviews of case reports, four of six by one author, in a literature where an MAOI is likely to be named whenever a severe case is written up; (3) might be lethal and nearly all are statements of likelihood without counts or denominators; (4) the figures for SSRI and moclobemide overdoses are from the authors’ own earlier papers, and the attenuation statement rests on one volunteer study not read here.

timeline.event: Dunkley and colleagues derive and test the Hunter criteria; the review’s only citation for validated.
Isbister and colleagues: moclobemide overdose, toxicokinetics and occurrence of serotonin toxicity (reference 15; as described in this review; not read).
Gillman’s review of MAOIs, opioids and serotonin toxicity, cited among the reviews of case reports (reference 10).
This review restates the conclusions of those reviews for general doctors.

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source from the group that produced the Hunter criteria; its generalisation about MAOIs matches the one in Gillman’s 2005 review, which it cites, so the two are not independent. No new case data are given.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that they have read the journal group’s policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare (p. 3).
funding.affiliations_note: Consultant toxicologists at the NSW Poisons Information Centre, the University of Sydney, Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and the University of Newcastle (p. 1). Two of the three authors (Dawson and Isbister) are authors of Dunkley and colleagues (2003), the source of the Hunter criteria the review calls validated, and seven of the 20 references (1, 5, 7, 8, 13, 15 and 16) include one or more of the three authors. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An independent prospective validation of the Hunter criteria in emergency departments against a reference diagnosis made blind to the rules; a systematic review of the case literature for each drug pair that states its search and counts the reports; and surveillance that counts the people exposed to each pair, so that the share of severe cases involving a monoamine oxidase inhibitor can be set against how often these inhibitors are taken with other serotonergic drugs.

domains.note: No methods section; 20 references chosen by the authors; the reviews it relies on are called systematic without their methods being described.

Some appraisal (the treatment evidence is called weak, and many interaction warnings are called unsupported), but the Hunter criteria are called validated on the strength of the derivation paper, and the cited reviews of case reports are not appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Seven of 20 references (1, 5, 7, 8, 13, 15, 16) include at least one of the three authors, including the sources of the Hunter criteria, the SSRI overdose figure and the moclobemide figure.

Uncertainty is marked (presumably, seem to, it is unclear, no evidence has been found, no clinical trials or other strong evidence for any treatment), and the animal-model basis of the spectrum figure is stated.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the diagnostic rules and the listed drug mixes
domains.note: The case against over-broad interaction warnings is argued well, but the evidence for the MAOI generalisation is one group’s data and reviews, and the attenuation statement for serotonin-releasing agents rests on a single volunteer study.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. There is no search method, and a third of the references are the authors’ own. It may be cited for how three toxicologists described the condition and its recognition in 2014 and for the drug classes they list; it may not be cited for the Hunter criteria being independently validated, for the share of severe cases that involve an MAOI as an established figure, or for any risk of a pair of drugs.

key_findings.finding: The review defines serotonin syndrome as a drug-induced cluster of dose-related adverse effects caused by raised serotonin in the central nervous system; it is also called serotonin toxicity because it covers a spectrum from mild to severe, depending, presumably, on how far serotonin is raised. It is described as potentially fatal and largely avoidable.
key_findings.locator: Standfirst; What is serotonin syndrome?, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug induced syndrome

key_findings.finding: Severe toxicity usually occurs only with a combination of two or more serotonergic drugs (even when each is at a therapeutic dose), one of which is generally an MAOI; moderate toxicity has been reported with an overdose of a single drug and occasionally from increasing therapeutic doses; in large case series of overdoses, moderate toxicity occurred in 15% of SSRI poisonings.
key_findings.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, same paragraph

key_findings.finding: Severe or life-threatening effects (rigidity and hyperthermia) are said to result only from stimulation of 5-HT2 receptors, and the drug classes implicated are largely serotonin precursors, agonists, releasers, reuptake inhibitors and MAOIs; a few interactions are clearly linked to classic cases although the mechanism is unclear.
key_findings.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, paragraph beginning Severe or life threatening effects (continues in the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Serotonin toxicity starts within hours of taking the drug or drugs; the classic triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (hyperthermia, tachycardia) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion); the acute onset of these features should prompt a search for a toxic explanation, alongside withdrawal, non-convulsive seizures and encephalitis.

In the authors’ group’s case series, moderate toxicity occurred in 15% of SSRI overdoses with no severe cases; toxicity did not occur in overdoses of moclobemide alone, but if a second serotonergic drug was taken toxicity was nearly always present and was severe in about half of these cases.
key_findings.locator: How does it present?, 2nd paragraph (references 5 and 15)
key_findings.note: The moclobemide series (reference 15) was not read for this library.

key_findings.finding: Box 1 lists drugs associated with moderate to severe serotonin toxicity. Under the heading monoamine oxidase inhibitors: phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid, isocarboxazid, moclobemide (a reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A), linezolid and methylene blue. Under the heading serotonin releasing agents: fenfluramine, sibutramine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, phentermine, ecstasy and cathinones, and, listed beneath it, serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, venlafaxine and related drugs, clomipramine and imipramine), the opioid analgesics pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan, and St John’s wort. Under miscellaneous: lithium, tryptophan and buspirone. The footnote says severe toxicity generally involves a combination of agents from different drug classes.

The diagnosis is clinical and plausible only after starting or increasing the dose (or overdose) of a potent serotonergic drug, or shortly after a second is added. Contributing drugs can be hard to identify because some have persistent activity (irreversible MAOIs) or long half-lives (fluoxetine) and may have been stopped weeks earlier; drugs not marketed as serotonergic, such as tramadol, fentanyl, linezolid and methylene blue, are described as a trap.
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) is the classic feature, forming the key components of the Hunter criteria, which the review says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited is Dunkley and colleagues (reference 13).
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning Some pathognomonic features)

key_findings.finding: Severe toxicity is characterised by a rapidly rising temperature and rigidity and is diagnosed on clinical grounds; investigations are of no diagnostic value except to diagnose complications; neuroleptic malignant syndrome is distinguished by slow onset over days, extrapyramidal features and rigidity, and no clonus.
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 4th paragraph (beginning Severe serotonin toxicity is characterised; it continues in the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Mild serotonin toxicity is difficult to tell from many medical conditions or other drug effects; people taking therapeutic SSRIs commonly have lower-limb hyperreflexia or a few beats of ankle clonus without toxicity; a diagnosis of mild serotonin syndrome may be tempting for any febrile, tachycardic, agitated or confused person on psychiatric drugs, and many reports quote the non-specific Sternbach criteria without the classic Hunter features.
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 5th paragraph (beginning A different problem relates to mild serotonin toxicity, right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: The treatment section states that there are no clinical trials or other strong evidence supporting any of the treatment approaches it describes, but that recovery is usual and mortality low (under 1%) when such approaches have been applied (references 5 and 15).
key_findings.locator: How can we treat it?, paragraph beginning Serotonin antagonists and in particular 5HT2A receptor antagonists (the sentence beginning There are no clinical trials, at the foot of the left-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Prevention section: spurious associations and cautions have proliferated, and product information impedes sensible decision support; interactions of an SSRI with any MAOI might be lethal; interactions with other serotonin reuptake inhibitors are likely to be minor (additive); interactions with serotonin-releasing agents such as amphetamines might even attenuate toxicity (one volunteer study, reference 18); many listed interactions have little or no evidence that serotonergic effects increase.
key_findings.locator: How can we prevent it?, 1st paragraph (beginning Several systematic reviews clarify)
key_findings.note: The statement on serotonin-releasing agents concerns an SSRI taken with a releasing drug, which is the subject of another reader’s claim on MDMA and antidepressants.

key_findings.finding: It is apparent from systematic reviews of case reports (references 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11) that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and the relatively small number of these can easily be committed to memory.
key_findings.locator: How can we prevent it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning An awareness of drugs with potent serotonergic effects)
key_findings.note: Four of the six cited reviews are by one author (Gillman); the one read for this library (Gillman 2005) gives only a one-sentence description of its search (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, p. 437).

key_findings.finding: Susceptibility differs between people but strong consistent pharmacogenetic associations have not been found; no evidence supports theories that dietary MAOI compounds cause serotonin toxicity in highly susceptible people.
key_findings.locator: How can we prevent it?, 3rd paragraph (beginning Some individuals seem to be more susceptible, right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Provenance and declarations: commissioned and externally peer reviewed; the authors have no relevant interests to declare; no funding statement.
key_findings.locator: Contributors, Competing interests and Provenance statements

key_findings.finding: Summary points: serotonin syndrome is the clinical manifestation of excess serotonin in the central nervous system, from therapeutic use or overdose of serotonergic drugs; the most severe cases involve drug interactions, particularly between MAOIs and serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin-releasing drugs; the diagnosis is clinical, suspected on the triad, with confirmation based largely on the neuromuscular features in the Hunter criteria; the spectrum runs from mild to life-threatening.

Figure 1 sets severe toxicity (an MAOI plus SSRI combination as the typical cause: rigidity, respiratory failure, coma, severe hyperthermia), moderate toxicity (SSRI overdose; sustained clonus, agitation, mydriasis, sweating and a low fever below 38.5 °C), mild toxicity (ecstasy use; inducible clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertension, tachycardia) and the least (SSRI in therapeutic use; brisk reflexes) against approximate multiples of serotonin efflux from animal models. Figure 2 is a flowchart of the Hunter criteria that gives yes at spontaneous clonus; inducible or ocular clonus with agitation, sweating or (hypertonia and temperature above 38 °C); or tremor with hyperreflexia.
key_findings.note: The multiples in Figure 1 are approximate figures from animal models; the typical-cause labels are the authors’ and carry no counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says the Hunter criteria have been validated, with a single citation, the paper that derived them; no independent test is cited. The derivation paper itself says the rules need validating in other settings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Validated is stronger than the evidence cited; two of the review’s three authors are authors of the derivation paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The review calls references 3, 4, 6, 9, 10 and 11 systematic reviews; four are by one author, and the one read for this library (reference 10, Gillman 2005) gives only a one-sentence description of its search (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, p. 437).
reporting_issues.consequence: Nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI is a conclusion from narrative reviews of published case reports, so it may reflect which cases were written up; it is not a rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The moclobemide statement (no toxicity with moclobemide alone; with a second serotonergic drug nearly always present and severe in about half) comes from the authors’ own earlier paper, reference 15, and gives no number of cases in this review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The numbers behind about half cannot be checked here; the source was not read for this library.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is headed as a spectrum with approximate multiples of serotonin efflux from animal models, and names ecstasy use as the typical cause of mild toxicity and an MAOI plus SSRI combination as the typical cause of severe toxicity, without a reference for the pairing of cause and severity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels read as findings but carry no counts or source for the pairings; they cannot be used to rank the danger of MDMA against other causes.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1–4 (full text: standfirst, all five sections, Box 1, summary points, Figures 1 and 2, declarations, reference list); the figures were checked against a page render. The treatment doses were read for context only and are not recorded. The cited primary sources were not read except Dunkley and colleagues (2003) and Gillman (2005).
